game.name: Microservice Cache TTL — Shared Backend Commons
game.description: Two microservices independently select a cache TTL (short ≈ 30 s, long ≈ 5 min) for calls to a shared backend. Short TTL produces fresher data but inflicts backend load that harms both services; long TTL conserves backend capacity but risks stale responses. Neither service can observe or bind the other's choice before deciding. This is a non-cooperative normal-form game.

payoffMatrix.description: Net operational utility per service (arbitrary units, higher = better). Components: freshness gain from short TTL = +3; backend saturation penalty when BOTH use short TTL = −5 each (timeouts, latency spikes, circuit-breaker trips); single-service backend load spillover cost = −1 per service (even the non-short-TTL service experiences degraded backend response when the other hammers it); staleness penalty for long TTL = −2; backend health bonus when BOTH use long TTL = +3 (healthy shared infra lifts throughput and tail-latency for everyone, more than offsetting the mild staleness penalty).

entries.narrative: Both hammer the backend. Each gets fresh data (+3) but the backend saturates (−5). Net: −2 each.
A free-rides: gets freshness (+3) while load stays light with only A using short (−1). B bears staleness (−2) AND A's backend spillover (−1): net −3. A earns +2.
Symmetric to (SL). B free-rides at +2; A bears staleness + spillover at −3.
Both accept mild staleness (−2) but the backend stays healthy, conferring a shared throughput bonus (+3). Net: +1 each.

nashEquilibria.verification: If B plays short_ttl: A earns −2 (short) vs −3 (long) → A will NOT switch to long (−2 > −3). If A plays short_ttl: B earns −2 (short) vs −3 (long) → B will NOT switch to long (−2 > −3). Neither player can improve by unilateral deviation. The equilibrium is STRICT because both inequalities are strict (no indifference). No other pure-strategy profile survives the same check: from (long, long), A gains +1 by switching to short (+2 > +1), so it is not a Nash equilibrium.

dominantStrategies.justification: Regardless of B's choice: if B plays short_ttl, A earns −2 (short) > −3 (long); if B plays long_ttl, A earns +2 (short) > +1 (long). Short TTL strictly dominates for A in both scenarios.

By the game's symmetry the payoffs are identical. If A plays short_ttl: B earns −2 (short) > −3 (long). If A plays long_ttl: B earns +2 (short) > +1 (long). Short TTL strictly dominates for B in both scenarios.

paretoAnalysis.dominanceMagnitude: +3 units for each player — mutual long TTL strictly Pareto-dominates the Nash equilibrium

Jointly optimal; no player can be made better off without harming the other from this point

paretoAnalysis.conclusion: The Nash equilibrium (−2, −2) is strictly Pareto-dominated. Both services would prefer the cooperative outcome but rational self-interest prevents it without an external coordination mechanism.

structuralComparison.canonicalGame: Prisoner's Dilemma (also: Tragedy of the Commons)

mapping.short_ttl: Defect — exploit the shared backend commons
mapping.long_ttl: Cooperate — restrain usage for mutual benefit

structuralComparison.payoffOrdering: For each player: (short | other=long) > (long | other=long) > (short | other=short) > (long | other=short), i.e., T > R > P > S = 2 > 1 > −2 > −3. This satisfies the Prisoner's Dilemma conditions T > R > P > S and 2R > T + S.
resolutionMechanisms: Platform-enforced TTL policy via service mesh or config management — converts the non-cooperative game into a cooperative one with binding rules
Shared rate-limiter / adaptive TTL controller on the backend — makes the load cost immediately visible and penalizes overuse in real time (internalizes the externality)
Circuit-breaker feedback loop — when backend degrades, both services are forced to long TTL, approximating the cooperative outcome emergently
Iterated game with reputation — if the services interact repeatedly and can observe each other's behavior, tit-for-tat strategies can sustain (long, long) as an equilibrium via the Folk Theorem

analysis: Yes — there is a unique Nash equilibrium: both services choose short TTL, yielding payoffs (−2, −2). Short TTL is a strictly dominant strategy for each service independently: no matter what the other service does, a service earns more by refreshing its cache aggressively. The tragedy is that this rational individual choice is collectively self-defeating. Mutual long TTL at (+1, +1) is strictly Pareto-superior — both services would be objectively better off — yet neither can unilaterally adopt long TTL without being exploited (earning −3 instead of −2). The game is a Prisoner's Dilemma over shared backend infrastructure, structurally identical to the Tragedy of the Commons. The Nash equilibrium is stable but inefficient. Breaking out requires a coordination mechanism external to the game: a service mesh TTL policy, an adaptive circuit breaker that makes backend load costs visible and immediate, or repeated-game dynamics with observable behavior that allow tit-for-tat strategies to stabilize mutual restraint.
